Experiments that changed questions

Skinner's superstitious pigeons

Food at fixed intervals, whatever they did. The pigeons ended up with rituals of their own.

In 1948, B. F. Skinner placed hungry pigeons in a box that released food every 15 seconds, regardless of their behaviour. When he came back, many were repeating odd movements: one turned in circles, another pushed its head into a corner, another swayed.

Coincidences that get reinforced

Skinner explained it like this: the pigeon happened to be doing something when the food arrived, and that behaviour was reinforced by chance, even though it had nothing to do with it. Repeating it made it likely to coincide with another delivery, and the habit took hold.

He compared it to gamblers' rituals or the bowler who "steers" the ball after releasing it. Later studies have qualified his interpretation, but the idea that coincidences can create beliefs is still useful.

References

  1. Skinner, B. F. (1948). 'Superstition' in the pigeon. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 38(2), 168–172.
  2. Staddon, J. E. y Simmelhag, V. L. (1971). The "superstition" experiment. Psychological Review, 78(1), 3–43.
